If you do specify custom priors, verify that they produce plausible data before you look at your own: `bmm(..., sample_prior = "only")` samples from the prior alone, and `pp_check()` on the result shows you what RT distributions your priors imply. We skip that step here because the defaults are calibrated for typical RT data, but it is not optional once you depart from them.

### Model Fitting

Fit the model with `bmm()`, which wraps `brms::brm()` with the model-specific likelihood. Setting `sample_prior = "yes"` stores prior samples, which the Savage-Dickey tests in the Hypothesis Testing section below require; `file` caches the fitted model to disk, so re-running the script does not re-fit it. `threads` splits each chain's likelihood evaluation across two cores, and the `control` arguments tune Stan's sampler: `adapt_delta` sets how cautiously the sampler takes steps (higher values mean smaller, safer steps) and `max_treedepth` caps how far a single step can travel. The values below are safe defaults for EAMs, and every subsequent tutorial reuses them.

```{r}
#| label: t1-fit
fit_acc_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_acc,
  data    = data_acc_ezdm,
  model   = model_acc,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  threads = threading(2),
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc")
)
```

Fitting completed in `r t1_time` with five parallel chains. Convergence should always be verified before interpreting results. The two key diagnostics are $\hat{R}$ (which should be below 1.01 for all parameters) and effective sample size (ESS, which should be at least 400 for reliable posterior summaries). Both can be inspected via `summary(fit_acc_ezdm)`, which displays these diagnostics for every parameter. For this model, the maximum $\hat{R}$ was `r round(t1_rhat, 3)` and the minimum bulk ESS was `r round(t1_ess)`, indicating that the chains mixed well and the posterior was adequately sampled.^[If convergence issues arise, standard remedies include increasing the number of iterations, raising `adapt_delta` (e.g., to 0.95 or 0.99), or simplifying the random-effects structure. See the Troubleshooting section in Practical Guidelines for details.]

### Model Evaluation

Before interpreting parameter estimates, we check whether the fitted model reproduces the data. For the EZ-Diffusion Model the data are three summary statistics per design cell, and `pp_check()` checks each of them. `pp_check_vars()` lists the observables a fitted model offers, and the `resp_var` argument selects one of them, or all of them at once:

```{r}
#| label: t1-ppcheck-code
pp_check_vars(fit_acc_ezdm)
pp_check(fit_acc_ezdm, resp_var = "all", ndraws = 50)
```

@fig-t1-ppcheck shows the three checks. For every design cell, the observed mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct (dark points) are plotted against the values simulated from the posterior (light intervals). A model that reproduced the cells would leave at most about one cell in ten outside its 90% interval. Here `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_rt"]]` of the `r lex_cells` cells fall outside it for mean RT, `r t1_ppc_out[["var_rt"]]` for the RT variance, and `r t1_ppc_out[["mean_pc"]]` for the proportion correct. With hundreds of trials per cell the predictive intervals are narrow, so the checks are sensitive: they show where the cell statistics depart from what the formula allows, in which ndt is shared by all of a participant's cells, bound by the two stimulus categories, and drift by the two emphasis conditions. One caveat is specific to the EZ-Diffusion Model: because it is fit to three summary statistics per cell rather than to individual RTs, its checks can only show whether those statistics are reproduced, and cannot detect misfit in the finer shape of the RT distribution. The trial-level Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, which model individual RTs (including the separate distributions of correct and error responses), yield more diagnostic checks; we return to these in Part II.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive checks for the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model fitted to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data, one panel per summary statistic: mean RT, RT variance, and proportion correct. Each dark point is the observed value of one participant × emphasis × stimulus-category cell; light bars show the 50% and 90% intervals of the values simulated from 50 posterior draws."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_pp_check.pdf"))
```

Extract the population-level estimates with `fixef()`:

```{r}
#| label: t1-params
#| eval: true
fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
```

Read this table one link function at a time. The two `drift_` rows use the identity link, so the `Estimate` column is already on the drift scale and can be read off directly. The `bound_` and `ndt_` rows use the log link, so their estimates are on the log scale and mean nothing until you exponentiate them. `Q2.5` and `Q97.5` bound the 95% credible interval, and they transform the same way — exponentiate the interval limits rather than trying to build an interval around the exponentiated mean.

```{r}
#| label: t1-params-transform
#| eval: true
exp(fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)[c("bound_conditionspeed", "bound_conditionaccuracy"), ])
```

This is the step you will repeat for every log-link parameter in every model below, so it is worth doing explicitly once rather than reaching for a helper.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion parameter estimates from the accuracy-coded analysis. Left: drift by stimulus category. Right: bound by emphasis condition. Points show posterior means; error bars show 95% credible intervals."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_param_estimates.pdf"))
```

The emphasis manipulation shows the expected effect on bound (@fig-t1-params): speed emphasis produced lower bound ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_speed`) than accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_acc`), reflecting reduced response caution. Drift estimates are nominally higher for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_word`) than nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_nonword`), but the difference is small; collapsing all words into a single category averages across high-, low-, and very-low-frequency items that differ strongly in drift, as the refit at the end of this tutorial shows. Non-decision time was estimated at $\tau$ = `r t1_ndt` seconds. The bound result already demonstrates the core value of EAMs: a traditional analysis comparing mean RTs could not distinguish whether speed-emphasis participants were faster because they processed evidence more efficiently or because they required less evidence. We return to drift effects at the frequency level below, and Part III compares the result with the full DDM's at the same specification.

### Hypothesis Testing

Because we fitted the model with `sample_prior = "yes"`, we can use `brms::hypothesis()` to test hypotheses about the condition effects via Savage-Dickey density ratios. Writing a hypothesis as an equality (e.g., `drift_word = drift_nonword`) asks how much the data changed our belief in *no difference*: the resulting `Evid.Ratio` compares the posterior to the prior density at a difference of zero, and its inverse is the Bayes Factor (BF) quantifying the evidence *against* equality. In other words, a BF of 10 means the data are ten times more likely under a model in which the two parameters differ than under one in which they are equal. As a rough guide, BFs above 3 indicate moderate evidence, above 10 strong evidence, and above 100 decisive evidence [@kass1995bayes]. All BFs reported in this tutorial follow this convention.

You can pass several hypotheses at once as a character vector, which keeps related tests together in one output table:

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, c(
  drift = "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword",
  bound = "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed"
))
```

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
t1_hyp
```

The column to read is `Evid.Ratio`. For `bound` it is far below 1, so its inverse — the evidence against equality — is decisive (BF = `r bf_fmt(t1_bf_bound)`): speed–accuracy emphasis unambiguously changes response caution.

For `drift` the test comes out the other way. The BF against equality is `r round(t1_bf_drift, 2)`, meaning the data favor *no difference* between words and nonwords by roughly `r round(1 / t1_bf_drift)` to 1. This does not contradict the parameter estimates — words do show nominally higher drift — but it tells us the collapsed word/nonword contrast is too coarse to separate drift reliably. The next subsection revisits the contrast at the frequency level.

Two lessons follow, and both generalize beyond this dataset. Bayes Factors can quantify evidence *for* the absence of a difference, which a significance test cannot; and a selective influence test is only as sharp as the stimulus contrast you specify.


### Refining the Contrast: Word Frequency

<!-- TODO(Gidon): the frequency refit (and script 15's 4par freq fit) summarise data_accuracy_clean / data_response_clean, i.e. data already filtered by the contaminant flags, whereas Tutorial 1's first fit and Tutorial 2 summarise the unfiltered data with the mixture/robust method. The two Tutorial 1 fits therefore differ in their input data as well as in the contrast. Decide whether to align them (needs script 01 to save the unfiltered trial-level data with freq, and a ~1 min refit). -->

The null result on drift invites a sharper test, and with the EZ-Diffusion Model a sharper test is cheap. @wagenmakers2008lexical distinguished three word frequencies (high, low, very low) alongside nonwords, and the `freq` column carries that four-level factor. Recomputing the summary statistics per frequency level and substituting `freq` for `stim_cat` in the drift formula is the entire change:

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq
# data_accuracy_clean: the trial-level data after the contaminant flags of the
# Data Preprocessing section, as used by the trial-level fits of Part II
data_acc_ezdm_freq <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "3par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian",
                       maxit = 500),
    .by = c(id, condition, freq)
  )

formula_acc_freq <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)

fit_acc_ezdm_freq <- bmm(
  formula = formula_acc_freq,
  data    = data_acc_ezdm_freq,
  model   = model_acc,
  # chains, cores, threads, warmup, iter, control: as in the Tutorial 1 fit
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc_freq")
)
```

The fit took `r t1f_time` and converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t1f_rhat, 3)`). The equality test on the two ends of the frequency scale settles the question the collapsed contrast could not:

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq-hypothesis
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm_freq, "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low")
```

```{r}
#| label: t1-freq-hypothesis-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
t1f_hyp
```

The evidence against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is `r bf_label(t1f_bf_drift)` (BF = `r bf_fmt(t1f_bf_drift)`). Drift does vary with stimulus quality; the null result above was a property of how the stimulus contrast was specified, not of the parameter. The rank order the fit recovers is `r t1f_drift_order` (HF, LF, VLF: high-, low-, and very-low-frequency words; NW: nonwords), and Part III compares it with the full DDM's. Two lessons follow. A selective influence test is only as sharp as the contrast you give it, and refining the contrast costs a minute with this model, which is what makes exploring the predictor structure with the EZ-Diffusion Model a habit worth forming before committing to a trial-level fit.

## Tutorial 2: Estimating Response Bias with the EZ-Diffusion Model (4par)

Tutorial 1 used accuracy coding, where "upper" means correct regardless of stimulus type. But what if we want to know whether participants are biased toward saying "word"? Response bias is a substantively important question in many domains: in lexical decision, word frequency creates an a priori expectation that biases responses toward "word"; in recognition memory, participants may adopt liberal or conservative response criteria; in clinical research, impulsive responding in ADHD may manifest as a shifted relative starting point rather than changed drift.

To estimate such biases you need two things: *response coding*, where "upper" always means a "word" response, and the 4-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm` 4par), which adds the relative starting point ($\zeta_r$) as a fourth parameter. The companion script for this tutorial is `scripts/12_tutorial2_ezdm_4par.R`.

### Model Specification

As introduced in the Data Preparation section, response coding changes the question the model answers — from "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward the *correct* answer?" to "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward saying *word*?" Drift is therefore positive for word stimuli and negative for nonwords. Bound and ndt retain their interpretations, but the key new parameter is the relative starting point $\zeta_r$: values above 0.5 indicate a tendency to say "word" before evidence accumulation has run its course, an *a priori response bias* that the accuracy-coded model could not detect.

The model object changes in two ways relative to Tutorial 1. Setting `version = "4par"` adds $\zeta_r$ to the estimated parameters, and `mean_rt` and `var_rt` now take a *pair* of column names rather than one each:

The four-parameter version needs the moments separately for each boundary. `version = "4par"` returns them as `mean_rt_upper`, `var_rt_upper`, `mean_rt_lower`, and `var_rt_lower`, and we use the robust statistics for the reason given under Trial-Count Constraint below:

```{r}
#| label: t2-data
data_resp_ezdm <- data_response |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "4par", method = "robust"),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: t2-model
model_resp <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
  var_rt   = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "4par"
)
```

That pairing is what makes the fourth parameter identifiable. With an unbiased starting point, responses at the two boundaries have the same mean and variance; a starting point closer to one boundary makes responses at that boundary faster and less variable than responses at the other. The 4par version recovers $\zeta_r$ from exactly this asymmetry, which is why it needs boundary-specific moments where the 3par version needed only one mean and one variance per cell.

The formula adds one line for the new parameter, and is otherwise the Tutorial 1 formula:

```{r}
#| label: t2-formula
formula_resp_ezdm <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

Note that $\zeta_r$ is written `zr` in the formula, and that it gets emphasis condition as a predictor: this asks whether participants shift their starting point when instructed to favor speed over accuracy.

### Model Fitting

Fitting uses the same `bmm()` call as Tutorial 1, with the response-coded summary statistics and the 4par model object substituted in. All sampler settings are unchanged, so we show only what differs:

```{r}
#| label: t2-fit
fit_resp_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_resp_ezdm,
  data    = data_resp_ezdm,
  model   = model_resp,
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp")
)
```

### Model Evaluation

Convergence was adequate (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2_rhat, 3)`). The posterior predictive checks (@fig-t2-ppcheck) follow Tutorial 1, now with mean RT and RT variance separately for "word" and "nonword" responses and the proportion of "word" responses. Depending on the statistic, between `r min(t2_ppc_out)` and `r max(t2_ppc_out)` of the `r t2_cells` cells fall outside their 90% intervals, so the four-parameter version leaves systematic misfit in the cell statistics as well.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive checks for the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model fitted to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data: mean RT and RT variance for word and nonword responses, and the proportion of word responses. Each dark point is the observed value of one design cell; light bars show the 50% and 90% intervals of the values simulated from 50 posterior draws."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_pp_check.pdf"))
```

As expected, drift reverses by stimulus category: positive for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_word`, evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary) and negative for nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_nonword`, evidence accumulates toward the "nonword" boundary). This sign reversal is a direct consequence of response coding; the same underlying evidence accumulation process is now expressed relative to the "word" boundary rather than the "correct" boundary. The $\zeta_r$ estimates reveal a small starting-point shift: $\zeta_r$ = `r t2_zr_acc_ci` under accuracy emphasis and $\zeta_r$ = `r t2_zr_speed_ci` under speed emphasis. The accuracy-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_acc` suggests a slight bias toward saying "word," while the speed-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_speed` is close to unbiased. These values are consistent with the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis ($\zeta_r$ = 0.497 for accuracy, 0.476 for speed), confirming that this dataset shows only a very small a priori response bias (@fig-t2-params).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion 4par parameter estimates from the response-coded analysis. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category, positive for word stimuli, negative for nonword stimuli. Middle: Bound estimates by emphasis condition. Right: Relative starting point by emphasis condition. Values near 0.5 indicate minimal response bias."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_resp_params.pdf"))
```

### Hypothesis Testing

Equality tests analogous to Tutorial 1 confirm the expected patterns. The Bayes Factors against zero drift for words (BF = `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_drift_word)`) and for nonwords (BF = `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_drift_nw)`), and against equal bound across emphasis conditions (BF = `r bf_fmt(t2_bf_bound)`), are all decisive. The selective influence pattern is robust to the change in response coding.

### Trial-Count Constraint

One practical limitation surfaced in this analysis, and it matters beyond this dataset. The `ezdm` 4par version requires enough trials on *both* boundaries in every cell. In this dataset, nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield very few "word" responses — median 17 per cell, minimum 1 — which makes the variance estimate for the minority boundary unreliable. `ezdm_summary_stats()` returns `NA` moments for a boundary with fewer than `min_trials` responses (10 by default), and a cell with `NA` moments drops out of the fit: `r t2_cells` of the `r lex_cells` cells entered it here. This is not a quirk of our preprocessing; it arises organically whenever a condition is easy enough that participants rarely err, and it is why we computed the 4par summary statistics with `method = "robust"` rather than `method = "mixture"`: the mixture method's EM step cannot converge on a cell containing a single observation.

The constraint is not merely a technical inconvenience. It points at a general limitation of summary-statistic approaches: when a cell contains very few responses on one boundary, the per-cell moments that the EZ-Diffusion Model requires stop being estimable, and no amount of care in preprocessing recovers them. Trial-level approaches sidestep the problem entirely, because they never form per-cell statistics: they evaluate a likelihood for each observation and borrow strength across participants through the hierarchical structure. Part II returns to them. Before that, the next section asks a question the lexical decision data cannot answer, because their starting point sits so close to 0.5: what does the four-parameter version buy when the starting point is in fact biased?


## Recovering a Biased Starting Point

The three-parameter model fixes $\zeta_r$ at 0.5. The lexical decision data barely test that assumption, because the estimated starting points sit within a few hundredths of 0.5 under both emphasis conditions. Many designs are less forgiving. Unequal stimulus proportions, payoff manipulations, and prior expectations all shift the starting point, and a model that fixes it has to absorb the shift elsewhere. To see what the four-parameter version buys under such conditions, and what ignoring the bias costs, we simulated data with a known, biased starting point and fitted both versions alongside the full DDM. The companion script is `scripts/22_bias_recovery.R`; the data are generated by `scripts/20_prepare_simulated_data.R`.

### Design

Fifty simulated participants completed a two-choice task with two stimulus types and two bias conditions (data columns `stimulus` and `bias`), `r bias_trials_per_cell` trials per cell. The stimulus type sets the direction of drift, positive for stimulus A and negative for stimulus B, so that with response coding (upper = an "A" response) both boundaries are reached often. The bias condition sets the relative starting point at 0.60 (toward the "A" boundary) or 0.40 (toward the "B" boundary). Bound (1.5) and non-decision time (0.3 s) did not vary by condition. Participant-level parameters were drawn around these population values with between-participant standard deviations of 0.25 on drift, 0.15 on log bound, 0.03 s on ndt, and 0.20 on the logit of $\zeta_r$; the drift spread is smaller than in the appendix's recovery study so that every cell keeps enough responses at its minority boundary for the boundary-specific moments the four-parameter model needs. We fitted the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model with a bias-condition effect on $\zeta_r$, the three-parameter model to the same cells with $\zeta_r$ fixed at 0.5, and the full DDM with the four-parameter formula:

```{r}
#| label: bias-formula
formula_bias <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stimulus + (0 + stimulus | id),
  bound ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + bias + (0 + bias | id)
)
```

### Results

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-recovery
#| fig-cap: "Group-level recovery with a biased starting point. Points are posterior means with 95% credible intervals for the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (starting point fixed at 0.5), and the full DDM; dashed lines mark the generating values. Panels show drift by stimulus type, bound, non-decision time, and the relative starting point by bias condition."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
if (bias_ok) {
  knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "22_bias_recovery_group.pdf"))
} else {
  ggplot() + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Figure pending: scripts/22_bias_recovery.R has not been run yet.") + theme_void()
}
```

@fig-bias-recovery shows the group-level estimates against the generating values. The four-parameter model estimated $\zeta_r$ = `r bias_zr_A` under the A-bias condition and `r bias_zr_B` under the B-bias condition, against generating values of 0.60 and 0.40; the full DDM estimated `r bias_ddm_zr_A` and `r bias_ddm_zr_B`. Drift for the two stimulus types was `r bias_drift_4par` in the four-parameter model, `r bias_drift_3par` in the three-parameter model, and `r bias_drift_ddm` in the full DDM, against generating values of ±`r bias_drift_true`. Bound was `r bias_bound_4par`, `r bias_bound_3par`, and `r bias_bound_ddm` respectively (generating value 1.5). None of the three fits met the convergence criteria of the Practical Guidelines for the population-level bound (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r bias_bound_rhat_max`, minimum bulk ESS = `r bias_bound_ess_min`), so the bound values are reported here but not interpreted. Subject-level correlations between generating and recovered values ranged from `r bias_r_min` to `r bias_r_max` across parameters and models (the appendix shows the scatter plots).

Not interpreted until Gidon decides on a refit (e.g. longer chains). Once converged: interpret the recovery. Directional claims (which model is biased where, whether the 3par absorbs the starting-point shift into drift or bound) are written only from the fitted values. -->

The fits took `r bias_time_4par` (four-parameter EZ-Diffusion), `r bias_time_3par` (three-parameter), and `r bias_time_ddm` (full DDM). That contrast, under two minutes for each EZ-Diffusion fit against hours for the full DDM on the same 50 participants, is the reason Part II fits the trial-level approaches once, at a specification the EZ-Diffusion Model has already explored, rather than developing the model at trial-level cost.


# Part II: Trial-Level Estimation

## Tutorial 3: The Censored-Shifted Wald and the Full DDM at the Same Specification

So far the EZ-Diffusion Model has worked with three numbers per cell. Trial-level modeling preserves the shape of the RT distribution, allows trial-level predictors, and handles sparse cells through hierarchical shrinkage rather than through per-cell variance estimates. The price is a likelihood evaluated for every trial. `bmm` offers two trial-level approaches. The Censored-Shifted Wald replaces the two-boundary process with one or two single-boundary shifted Wald accumulators [@anders2016shifted; @heathcote2004fitting], and its simple version is the only trial-level fit that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM (Part III reports the timings). The full DDM evaluates the Wiener first-passage time distribution, with its infinite series, for every trial; it is the mathematically complete characterization of the process and the reference against which the other approaches are judged. This tutorial fits both, together with the competing-risks version of the Censored-Shifted Wald, at the specification Part I arrived at, four frequency levels on drift, so that Part III can compare the three approaches parameter by parameter. The companion scripts are `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R` and `scripts/14_tutorial4_ddm.R`.

The `bmm` workflow is unchanged. What differs from Part I is the model object (`cswald()` or `ddm()` instead of `ezdm()`) and the data: the trial-level `rt` and `response` columns instead of aggregated summary statistics. The `response` column must contain the values `"upper"` and `"lower"`, identifying which boundary each trial reached, which is the coding applied in the Data Preparation section.

### Preparing Trial-Level Data

The cleaned trial-level data from the Data Preprocessing section are the input. One property of the trial-level likelihoods concerns which trials should be in the data at all. Both the shifted Wald density and the Wiener density are zero for any RT shorter than the non-decision time. A trial faster than ndt therefore does not merely fit poorly; it has no likelihood, and the sampler responds by forcing ndt below the fastest surviving RT, with bound and drift absorbing the consequences. Under the simple Censored-Shifted Wald an *error* faster than ndt behaves differently. It contributes the log survival function, which at an RT below ndt equals zero, the largest value that term can take, and so pushes ndt upward. The mixture flags of `flag_contaminant_rts()` do not target this region, because the EM knows nothing about ndt; what removes such trials is a lower RT cutoff. The lexical decision data already carry one, since `censor == FALSE` applies the original study's bounds of 180 ms and 3 s, and the fastest RT in the cleaned data is `r min_rt_ms` ms. If your own data do not, apply a lower cutoff before any trial-level fit, at a value below any plausible non-decision time for your task, and leave the slow tail to the mixture flags.

Before comparing estimates against published ones, one point about the scale of DDM parameters needs stating, because it silently invalidates comparisons that ignore it. DDM parameters are defined only relative to a scaling constant: multiplying drift, bound, and the diffusion noise $s$ by the same factor leaves the predicted data unchanged. `bmm` and Stan fix $s = 1$, whereas older software often used $s = 0.1$. Reference values drawn from that older literature must therefore be rescaled, by a factor of 10, before they can be compared with `bmm` output. All reference values we quote below have been converted to $s = 1$.

### Model Specification

The Censored-Shifted Wald model object needs the RT column, the response column, and the version:

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-simple
model_simple <- cswald(
  rt       = "rt",
  response = "response",
  version  = "simple"
)
```

The *simple* version treats errors as censored observations, in the sense set out in the Background: each error tells the model only that the correct-boundary process had not finished by the observed RT. Because censored trials constrain the parameters less than completed ones, this version needs errors to stay reasonably rare, and @miller2018shifted put the guideline at 20%. The lexical decision data test that guideline once the four frequency levels are separated. Accuracy-coded error rates run from `r err_min`% (high-frequency words under accuracy emphasis) to `r err_second`% (low-frequency words under speed emphasis) in seven of the eight emphasis × frequency cells, and reach `r err_max`% for very-low-frequency words under speed emphasis. We keep the frequency specification for comparability with the other two approaches, and Part III reports whether the approximation's known weak point, the boundary estimate, deviates more in that cell.

The *competing-risks* (crisk) version models errors explicitly: two accumulators race, one per response boundary, sharing a single non-decision time, and whichever finishes first produces the observed response. Nothing is left as a lower bound, which is what allows this version to estimate the relative starting point $\zeta_r$, and it carries no error-rate guideline. We apply it to the response-coded data, where it can estimate $\zeta_r$ and handle the unbalanced boundary counts that limited the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach.

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-crisk
model_crisk <- cswald(
  rt       = "rt",
  response = "response",
  version  = "crisk"
)
```

The full DDM's model object is the simplest of the three. `ddm()` needs only the RT and response columns; there is no `version` argument, because the full DDM has one form, and $\zeta_r$ is included or omitted by whether the formula supplies a `zr` line.

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-ddm
model_ddm <- ddm(rt = "rt", response = "response")
```

Two formulas serve all four fits. For the accuracy-coded analysis, all drifts are positive: they measure evidence toward the correct boundary regardless of stimulus type. A consequence worth anticipating is that the drift rank order differs from the response-coded model. High-frequency words have the highest drift, but nonwords, which are relatively easy to reject, have higher drift than very-low-frequency words, which are difficult to recognize. The expected rank order from @wagenmakers2008lexical is HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > NW (2.64) > VLF (1.80). This formula is passed to the simple Censored-Shifted Wald and to the full DDM:

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-acc
formula_trial_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

For the response-coded analysis, drift sign reflects the stimulus: positive for words, where evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary, and negative for nonwords. The expected values are HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > VLF (1.80) > 0 > NW (−2.64). Adding a `zr` line lets $\zeta_r$ capture any bias toward saying "word"; the reference values suggest a very small shift between conditions ($\zeta_r$ = 0.497 accuracy, 0.476 speed). This formula is passed to the competing-risks version and to the full DDM:

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-resp
formula_trial_resp <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

### Model Fitting

We show the first call in full; the other three differ only in formula, data, model object, and output file. Sampler settings are those of Part I, and every fit in this tutorial ran with two threads per chain, one fit at a time, so that the timings Part III reports are comparable across approaches (see the note to @tbl-model-comparison).

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit-simple
fit_cswald_simple <- bmm(
  formula = formula_trial_acc,
  data    = data_accuracy_clean,
  model   = model_simple,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  threads = threading(2),
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit-others
fit_cswald_crisk <- bmm(
  formula = formula_trial_resp, data = data_response_clean, model = model_crisk,
  file = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp")
)
fit_ddm_acc <- bmm(
  formula = formula_trial_acc, data = data_accuracy_clean, model = model_ddm,
  file = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc")
)
fit_ddm_resp <- bmm(
  formula = formula_trial_resp, data = data_response_clean, model = model_ddm,
  file = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp")
)
```

We set `adapt_delta = 0.90` and `max_treedepth = 12` for both the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM to reduce divergent transitions and max-treedepth warnings. If you fit trial-level models of your own, start from these values rather than the `brms` defaults.

### Model Evaluation

All four models converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_simple, 3)` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, `r round(t3_rhat_crisk, 3)` for the competing-risks version, `r round(t4_rhat_acc, 3)` and `r round(t4_rhat_resp, 3)` for the accuracy- and response-coded DDM). The posterior predictive checks (@fig-trial-ppcheck) cover the three observables of the trial-level likelihoods: the RT distribution, the response proportions, and the signed RT, which places lower-boundary responses on the negative axis and so checks choices and RTs jointly. Unlike the checks in Part I, they can show misfit in the shape of the distribution, because these models are fitted to individual RTs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trial-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive checks for the four trial-level fits to the Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data: the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (accuracy-coded), the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald (response-coded), and the full DDM under both codings. One row per fit; the columns show the response time, the response (lower = 0, upper = 1), and the signed response time (lower-boundary responses negative). Dark: observed data; light: data simulated from 50 posterior draws."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
if (file.exists(here("figures", "15_pp_check_trial_level.pdf"))) {
  knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_pp_check_trial_level.pdf"))
} else {
  ggplot() + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Figure pending: scripts/15_cross_model_comparison.R produces the composite check after the refit.") + theme_void()
}
```

One point about scale comes before the estimates, because it is easy to get wrong. The simple version has only one boundary, and what it estimates as bound is the distance from the starting point to that boundary. With an unbiased starting point this is *half* the boundary separation that `ezdm` and `ddm` report, so `cswald(version = "simple")` estimates must be multiplied by 2 before they are compared with the other two approaches or with published values; nothing in the output marks the difference. We do so throughout, and the scripts apply the same factor. The conversion is a matter of definition, not of accuracy. On data simulated from a known diffusion process, fitting the `bmm` simple likelihood returns a bound close to half the generating separation, as the definition predicts, but the doubled estimate is not thereby an unbiased estimate of $\alpha$: bound is the parameter the single-boundary approximation has the weakest claim on, because collapsing two boundaries into one is precisely an assumption about the boundaries. The crisk version needs no conversion; it estimates the full separation directly.

Under accuracy coding, the simple Censored-Shifted Wald put bound, converted to the full-boundary scale, at `r t3s_bound_acc` under accuracy emphasis and `r t3s_bound_speed` under speed emphasis; the full DDM put it at `r t4_bound_acc` and `r t4_bound_speed`. Drift by stimulus level was `r t3s_drift_txt` for the simple version and `r t4_drift_txt` for the full DDM, and non-decision time `r t3s_ndt` s and `r t4_ndt` s. Under response coding, the competing-risks version estimated $\zeta_r$ = `r t3c_zr_acc` under accuracy emphasis and `r t3c_zr_speed` under speed emphasis, and the full DDM `r t4_zr_acc` and `r t4_zr_speed`. Both recover the drift sign reversal seen in the EZ-Diffusion 4par. The competing-risks version also handled without complaint the sparse minority-boundary cells that forced the EZ-Diffusion 4par onto the robust aggregation method: because it evaluates a likelihood per trial rather than moments per cell, a cell with one "word" response is simply a cell with one observation.


### Hypothesis Testing

As in Part I, we quantify the evidence with equality tests. The Bayes Factor against equal bound across emphasis conditions is `r bf_label(t4_bf_bound)` for the full DDM (BF = `r bf_fmt(t4_bf_bound)`) and `r bf_label(t3_bf_bound)` for the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (BF = `r bf_fmt(t3_bf_bound)`), reproducing the conclusion Part I reached in seconds. The full DDM's Bayes Factor against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is `r bf_label(t4_bf_drift)` (BF = `r bf_fmt(t4_bf_drift)`), the same verdict the EZ-Diffusion refit of Tutorial 1 returned in a minute.

### When to Use Which Version

Use the simple version when error rates are low, below roughly 20%, and your research question does not require the relative starting point. On the lexical decision data it kept the word-frequency ordering of drift, but its drift estimates ran `r simple_drift_lo`% to `r simple_drift_hi`% above the full DDM's, and its bound, even after the factor of 2 described above, ran `r bound_simple_excess["accuracy"]`% to `r bound_simple_excess["speed"]`% above (Part III). It is the only version of the Censored-Shifted Wald that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM. Use the competing-risks version when error rates are higher, when $\zeta_r$ is of interest, or when response coding is used. It costs most of what the full DDM costs, so it is a choice about what you want to estimate rather than a way to save time. On these data its estimates were close to the full DDM's, bound included, which differed by at most `r bound_crisk_diff`%; on the simulated data of the appendix, however, it placed bound `r rec_crisk_bound_pct`% below the generating value, where the full DDM recovered it. The simple version's bound, then, is not an absolute value to take at face value. The direction of the boundary effect was the same under every approach in our analyses (Part III), so questions about the *direction* of a boundary effect are safe; if your question concerns its precise magnitude, prefer the full DDM.


# Part III: Comparison and Practical Guidelines

## Cross-Approach Comparison

Having applied all three DDM estimation approaches to the same dataset at the same specification, we can answer a question that is difficult to answer without a unified framework: does the EZ-Diffusion Model reach the full DDM's conclusions, and where do the approximations break down? Agreement validates the faster approaches against the reference; disagreement shows where the computational savings come at a substantive cost. We start with the cost, because it is what the comparison is for.

### Computational Cost

The fitting times on the present dataset span three orders of magnitude. The EZ-Diffusion fits took `r cost_ezdm_range`, the simple Censored-Shifted Wald `r cost_cswald_simple`, the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald `r cost_cswald_crisk`, and the full DDM `r cost_ddm_range` (wall-clock of the slowest of five parallel chains, two threads per chain, one fit at a time). Two features of this hierarchy matter for how the approaches should be used. First, the EZ-Diffusion Model provides in minutes what takes the full DDM the better part of a day: for the accuracy-coded frequency specification the factor is `r cost_factor`. Second, the computational saving of the Censored-Shifted Wald lies mainly in its simple version, which took `r cost_simple_share`% of the accuracy-coded full DDM's time. The competing-risks version took `r cost_crisk_share`% of the response-coded full DDM's time, so it should be chosen for what it estimates, a relative starting point at higher error rates, not for speed.

### Accuracy-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-acc
#| fig-cap: "Cross-approach comparison of accuracy-coded parameter estimates at the four-level frequency specification. Panels show drift by word-frequency level, bound by emphasis condition, and non-decision time for the EZ-Diffusion Model, the simple Censored-Shifted Wald (bound converted to the full-boundary scale), and the full DDM. Error bars show 95% credible intervals; X markers show the reference values of Wagenmakers et al. (2008), rescaled to s = 1."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_accuracy.pdf"))
```

@fig-comparison-acc shows the accuracy-coded estimates side by side. All three approaches converge on the same substantive picture: emphasis changes bound in the same direction, and drift differs strongly across word-frequency levels, in the same order for the three word levels (high > low > very low). Low-frequency words and nonwords sit close together in all three, and the full DDM places nonwords marginally above low-frequency words. The conclusions hold whether the model consumed summary statistics (EZ-Diffusion), a single-boundary approximation (Censored-Shifted Wald), or the full Wiener likelihood (DDM).

Where the approaches diverge, they diverge in absolute values (@tbl-cross-model-acc reports the parameters all three share). The EZ-Diffusion Model's drift estimates differ from the full DDM's by `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% on average (`r t4_drift_pct_lo`% to `r t4_drift_pct_hi`% across frequency levels). Relative to known generating values, EZ-Diffusion drift is *attenuated* at high values when trial-to-trial variability is present [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]; relative to the full DDM fitted to the same empirical data, it ran at or above the DDM's here, most for high-frequency words. What matters for practice is that the condition differences keep their sign and order. For bound, once the simple Censored-Shifted Wald estimates are put on the full-boundary scale, the three approaches order themselves the same way under both emphasis conditions: the EZ-Diffusion Model lowest, the full DDM in between, and the simple Censored-Shifted Wald highest. The simple version sits `r bound_simple_excess["accuracy"]`% above the full DDM under accuracy emphasis and `r bound_simple_excess["speed"]`% above under speed emphasis. Speed emphasis contains the one cell above the 20% error guideline, very-low-frequency words at `r err_max`% errors, but bound is estimated per emphasis condition, so the fit cannot attribute the larger deviation to that cell. Drift is estimated per frequency level, and there the cell does leave a trace: the simple version's drift exceeded the full DDM's most for very-low-frequency words, the level that contains it. The EZ-Diffusion Model sits `r bound_ez_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez_deficit["speed"]`% below the full DDM and closest to the published values (1.59 and 0.84). Non-decision time was estimated at `r t4_ndt_ez` s by the EZ-Diffusion Model, `r t4_ndt_ddm` s by the full DDM, and `r t3s_ndt` s by the simple Censored-Shifted Wald, against a published 0.408 s; the Limitations section returns to why the trial-level estimates sit lower.


All of these divergences concern the absolute parameter scale. On the two questions applied work asks, does the manipulation change the parameter, and do individuals differ from one another, the approaches agree. That distinction is developed in the Practical Guidelines.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-model-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy-coded parameter estimates (posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale) for the parameters the three approaches share: bound by emphasis condition and ndt. Bound and ndt are back-transformed from the log link. Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) bound estimates are multiplied by 2 to convert them from the single-boundary scale to the full boundary separation the other two approaches report. Drift is compared in @fig-comparison-acc."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
.g3 <- function(fe, row, d = 2, m = 1) fmt_est(exp(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]) * m, d)
cross_tab_acc <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("Bound, speed ($\\alpha$)", "Bound, accuracy ($\\alpha$)", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)"),
  `EZ-Diffusion`    = c(.g3(fe_t4f,  "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4f,  "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4f,  "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Censored-Shifted Wald (simple)` = c(.g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed", m = 2), .g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy", m = 2), .g3(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Full DDM`        = c(.g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", 3))
)
knitr::kable(cross_tab_acc, align = "lccc")
```

### Response-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-resp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-approach comparison of response-coded parameter estimates. Left: drift by word-frequency level; all three approaches show positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords. Middle: bound by emphasis condition. Right: relative starting point by emphasis condition; all three approaches estimate values close to 0.5. Error bars show 95% credible intervals."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_response.pdf"))
```

The response-coded comparison (@fig-comparison-resp) evaluates whether the approaches agree on two patterns: the drift sign reversal by stimulus category and the starting-point shift under speed emphasis. All three approaches recover the expected drift pattern, positive for word stimuli, negative for nonwords, so the response-coding interpretation is robust across estimation approaches. The relative starting point $\zeta_r$ estimates are close to 0.5 across approaches and emphasis conditions, consistent with the small bias reported in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis. In bound, the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald agreed with the full DDM to within `r bound_crisk_diff`%, while the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model placed it `r bound_ez4_deficit["accuracy"]`% and `r bound_ez4_deficit["speed"]`% lower, as the three-parameter version did under accuracy coding. The four-parameter fit at this specification rests on sparse cells: with the robust method and `min_trials = 3`, `r ez4f_cells` of the `r lex_cells_freq` cells had enough responses at both boundaries to enter it, and some of those estimate a boundary's variance from three responses.

Taken together, the comparison supports the position Part I argued for. For research questions about drift and about the direction of effects on bound and $\zeta_r$, the EZ-Diffusion Model is a primary analysis, not a screening step. When the absolute values of bound or $\zeta_r$ are central, for example when estimates are compared against published values, or when the shape of the RT distribution is itself the question, the full DDM is preferable, with the simple Censored-Shifted Wald as the affordable trial-level middle ground for high-accuracy data.


## Practical Guidelines

### Things to Keep in Mind

Before the approach-specific recommendations, here are the requirements and conventions that apply whichever approach you use. Most of them have caused us or our students trouble at some point.

- **RTs must be in seconds.** `bmm` does not inspect or convert your RT scale, and the default priors on ndt assume seconds. If your data are in milliseconds, divide by 1000 before fitting.
- **The response column must contain `"upper"` and `"lower"`.** Decide deliberately which coding you want: accuracy coding (upper = correct) tests selective influence, response coding (upper = one specific response) reveals decision bias. They answer different questions from the same trials.
- **Bound and ndt are estimated on the log scale, and `zr` on the logit scale.** The simple Censored-Shifted Wald also estimates drift on the log scale, because the drift of its single accumulator toward the correct boundary must be positive; the other approaches estimate drift on its natural scale. Back-transform with `exp()` and `plogis()` before interpreting or plotting anything, including credible-interval limits.
- **`cswald(version = "simple")` reports bound on the single-boundary scale.** It is the distance from the starting point to the correct boundary, half of what `ezdm`, `ddm`, and `cswald(version = "crisk")` report. Multiply by 2 before comparing it with any of them or with published values. Nothing in the output signals the difference, which makes it easy to compare two numbers that are not on the same scale.
- **Parameters are defined only up to a scaling constant.** `bmm` fixes the diffusion noise at $s = 1$; older software often used $s = 0.1$. Rescale published values before comparing.
- **Check convergence before you interpret anything.** $\hat{R}$ below 1.01 and bulk ESS above 400 for every parameter you intend to report; `summary()` shows both.
- **Respect the trial-count minima** (@tbl-model-comparison): roughly 30 per cell for the EZ-Diffusion Model, which needs stable variance estimates, and roughly 50 for the trial-level approaches [@lerche2017trials; @boag2025expert].
- **Preprocess with the mixture tools, not with hard cutoffs.** For `ezdm`, use `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture", maxit = 500)`; for the trial-level approaches, use `flag_contaminant_rts()` and a lower RT cutoff below any plausible non-decision time, because the trial-level likelihoods assign zero density to RTs faster than ndt (Part II).
- **ndt must fall below the fastest observed RT.** If ndt estimates sit suspiciously close to your minimum RT, read the Limitations section before interpreting them.

### When to Use Which Approach

The choice among the three estimation approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison) should be guided by the research question and stage of analysis:

- **EZ-Diffusion Model** (`ezdm`): Best for rapid exploration and designs with many conditions. For condition effects on drift it is also a viable primary analysis in its own right, not merely a screening step, as Part I and the Cross-Approach Comparison show. Use 3par by default; 4par when starting-point bias is expected. Requires ~30 trials per cell for stable variance estimates [@lerche2017trials; @lerche2016model].

- **Censored-Shifted Wald** (`cswald`): Choose the version by what you need, not by speed. The simple version is the trial-level approach for high-accuracy data: below roughly 20% errors the one-boundary approximation holds well, and this is the only version that is genuinely cheap (`r cost_cswald_simple` here), which is what makes iterative trial-level model development affordable. Remember that its bound is on the single-boundary scale and needs doubling before any comparison. The competing-risks version is what you need when error rates are higher or when the relative starting point is of interest; on these data it yielded parameters close to the full DDM's, bound included, but it costs most of what the full DDM costs (`r cost_crisk_share`% here).

- **Full DDM** (`ddm`): Gold standard for confirmatory analysis. Plan for fitting times of many hours (`r cost_ddm_range` here; see @tbl-model-comparison).

These recommendations rest on a distinction worth making explicit, about what "accurate estimation" should mean in practice. Outside of simulations, the true absolute parameter values are unknown; there is no reference to recover. The criteria that carry applied work are therefore different: an estimation approach must detect differences between experimental conditions or groups, and it must separate individuals reliably [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. On both criteria the three approaches converge in our analyses; condition effects replicated across approaches (Cross-Approach Comparison), and subject-level estimates correlated highly with their generating values for all three (see the appendix). The absolute-scale biases documented above are, in this sense, primarily a theoretical rather than a practical problem; they matter when estimates are compared against published values or interpreted as measurements on an absolute scale.

### Recommended Workflow

For condition effects on drift, bound, and the starting point, and for individual differences in them, fit the EZ-Diffusion Model and report it; Part I and the Cross-Approach Comparison are the case for treating it as the primary analysis. Move to a trial-level approach when the question needs what summary statistics discard: the shape of the RT distribution, trial-level predictors, cells too sparse for per-cell moments, or absolute values of bound. When you do, a staged workflow keeps the cost down. Iterating on the predictor structure is cheap with the EZ-Diffusion Model and the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple), and, as the Cross-Approach Comparison showed, the faster approaches are trustworthy guides for the drift-focused questions that dominate EAM applications. Divergences that follow the patterns documented here, amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, a lower EZ-Diffusion bound, and a higher bound from the doubled simple Censored-Shifted Wald, are expected. A divergence *beyond* them, such as a reversed effect or a qualitatively different rank order, signals a potential problem (model misspecification, data-quality issues) worth investigating before you finalize the analysis.

1. **Explore and refine with the EZ-Diffusion Model** (`ezdm`): Screen condition effects and settle the predictor structure, as Tutorial 1 did by moving from a two-level to a four-level stimulus contrast.

2. **Develop with the Censored-Shifted Wald, simple version** (`cswald`): Move to trial-level modeling here, where each iteration costs `r cost_cswald_simple` rather than `r cost_ddm_range` on data of this size. Refine the predictor structure, test different random-effects specifications, and evaluate prior sensitivity. Note that this stage is only available to you if error rates are below ~20%; above that, development has to happen at competing-risks or full-DDM cost.

3. **Confirm with the full DDM** (`ddm`): Fit the final model specification using the full DDM likelihood for confirmatory analysis.

4. **Cross-validate**: Compare Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM estimates as a robustness check.

Throughout all stages, preprocess with `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture", maxit = 500)` for `ezdm` fitting and with `flag_contaminant_rts()` plus a lower RT cutoff for trial-level fitting (Part II).

Adequate trial counts are essential for all approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison). The EZ-Diffusion Model is particularly sensitive because it relies on variance estimates, which stabilize more slowly than means [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @lerche2017trials]. For the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, @boag2025expert recommend at least 50 trials per condition for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.

### Prior Selection

All tutorials used `bmm`'s default priors, which differ between the approaches. The EZ-Diffusion Model and the full DDM place Cauchy(0, 1) on drift, Normal(0, 0.5) on bound (log link), and Normal(-1.5, 0.5) on ndt (log link). The Censored-Shifted Wald places Normal(0, 1) on drift (on the log scale in the simple version), Normal(0, 0.3) on bound and Normal(-2, 0.3) on ndt (both log link), and Normal(0, 0.3) on $\zeta_r$ in the competing-risks version (logit link). These priors are moderately informative and calibrated for typical data. Defaults can be inspected via `default_prior(formula, data, model)` and overridden using `brms::prior()`:

```{r}
#| label: priors-custom
custom_priors <- prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", dpar = "drift") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "bound")
```

When specifying custom priors, verify that they generate plausible RT data with a prior predictive check, fit with `sample_prior = "only"` and inspect `pp_check()`, and tighten them if the predictions are implausible.

### Common Issues and Troubleshooting

Convergence problems respond to the standard `brms`/Stan remedies: raise `adapt_delta`, increase iterations, simplify the random-effects structure, or fix $\zeta_r$ at 0.5. See the `brms` documentation for details [@burkner2017brms]. Two issues are EAM-specific. The mixture EM in `ezdm_summary_stats()` and `flag_contaminant_rts()` can stop at its default iteration cap of 100 before converging (on the lexical decision data it did so in 4 of 68 cells); the first function then silently returns the robust statistics (`contaminant_prop = NA`) and the second returns `NA` probabilities, which a `filter()` on the probability drops together with the entire cell. Pass `maxit = 500` and check that no cell has `NA` in `contaminant_prop`. The other issue: if the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM disagree on bound, check first that the simple version's estimates have been doubled onto the full-boundary scale, and then treat the remaining gap as the expected deviation (the doubled simple estimate above the DDM's; see Part II) rather than a fitting problem. Use the full DDM when boundary separation is the primary research question.


# Summary and Discussion

This tutorial applied three approaches for estimating DDM parameters, the EZ-Diffusion Model, the Censored-Shifted Wald, and full DDM likelihood estimation, to empirical data from a classic lexical decision experiment, all within `bmm`. Three tutorials ran the same three-step workflow with a different model object each time, which is the practical point of a unified interface: what you learn about specifying and interpreting one approach transfers to the others.

Three themes ran through them. First, data preprocessing is a substantive decision rather than housekeeping. `bmm`'s mixture tools handle the contaminants that sit away from the decision process, and the ones that overlap it have to be prevented by design. Second, the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model is a primary analysis in its own right. On the lexical decision data it reached the full DDM's conclusions on every condition effect we tested, and it did so in minutes where the trial-level approaches took hours; the recovery study with a biased starting point (Part I) shows what its four-parameter version recovers and what fixing the starting point costs. Third, response coding determines what questions a model can answer: accuracy coding tests selective influence, response coding reveals decision bias, and the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach runs into practical constraints when boundary trial counts are unbalanced, which the trial-level approaches do not share.

<!-- TODO(refit): the recovery clause in theme 2 is a placeholder until scripts/22 has run. -->

Two qualifications remain. First, clean convergence in sparse cells reflects hierarchical shrinkage: estimates for cells with only a handful of minority-boundary responses are pulled toward the group-level prior and should be read as regularized rather than data-driven. Second, when the research question concerns the shape of the RT distribution (e.g., leading-edge effects, the relative speed of errors) or the absolute values of bound or ndt, the full DDM remains the appropriate choice, with the Censored-Shifted Wald as the trial-level middle ground. For the more common targets, condition effects and individual differences, the estimation biases of the faster approaches are a theoretical rather than a practical concern [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Prior simulation work also reports statistical power for detecting condition effects comparable to or higher than the full DDM's [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]; we did not re-evaluate that result, but it is consistent with the convergence we observed.

## Limitations

Within the scope defined in the Introduction, the simple DDM framework and two-choice tasks, several aspects were not demonstrated. We did not show between-trial variability parameters ($s_v$, $s_\zeta$, $s_\tau$), which can improve fit but create identifiability challenges [@luken2025identifiability; @boag2025expert]; if you need the full seven-parameter DDM, consider alternatives such as HDDM [@wiecki2013hddm] or a custom Stan implementation. We also did not cover formal model comparison; bridge sampling and leave-one-out cross-validation are available via `brms` but were beyond the present scope.

One of these omissions deserves more than a mention, because it affects how the ndt estimates in this tutorial should be read. Trial-to-trial variability in non-decision time ($s_\tau$) has a specific consequence for the two trial-level approaches: both the shifted Wald likelihood and the Wiener likelihood require ndt to fall below the fastest observed RT, as Part II explained. When ndt in fact varies from trial to trial but is modeled as constant, its estimate is pinned to the leading edge of the RT distribution, and the remaining parameters can absorb the misfit [@miller2018shifted]. This is a plausible contributor to the ndt ordering we observed in the Cross-Approach Comparison.

The three approaches are not equally exposed. A forthcoming `bmm` extension relaxes the constraint for the Censored-Shifted Wald by adding an explicit uniform trial-to-trial ndt component (`sndt`) to the likelihood. The full DDM in `bmm` cannot be extended the same way: it relies on Stan's internal `wiener_lpdf()`, which provides no term for non-decision-time variability, and adding one requires the seven-parameter DDM, whose across-trial convolutions are prohibitively slow for hierarchical Bayesian estimation. The EZ-Diffusion Model is comparatively robust, because it recovers ndt from the mean rather than the minimum RT, so realistic trial-to-trial variability leaves its parameter recovery largely intact [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. This is one of the few respects in which the fastest approach is also the most forgiving.

Having worked through this tutorial, you are equipped to estimate DDM parameters from your own two-choice RT data, following the guidelines in Part III. The `bmm` package covers measurement models well beyond the DDM and continues to expand; the resources below are the natural next steps.

# References


# Parameter Recovery on Simulated Data {.appendix}

## When to Assess Parameter Recovery

Parameter recovery is not mandatory for every analysis, but it is informative as part of a principled Bayesian workflow — particularly when you apply a model to a new design for the first time, when trial counts per cell are unusual or unbalanced, or when individual-level estimates will feed into correlations. Beyond validating a given design, recovery simulations can inform experimental planning: by systematically varying the number of participants or trials, you can determine what your design needs to achieve acceptable recovery for the parameters you care about. For the EZ-Diffusion Model a single recovery run costs minutes, so there is little reason not to do it; for the trial-level approaches, budget the fitting times reported in @tbl-model-comparison.

The study reported here, with an unbiased starting point and an easy and a hard condition, verifies that the three `bmm` DDM estimation approaches produce reliable estimates, and complements the extensive parameter recovery literature for DDMs [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @lerche2016model]. The companion script is `scripts/21_appendix_parameter_recovery.R`.

## Simulation Design

We generated data from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for easy, 1.0 for hard; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3; $\zeta_r$: 0.5) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. Individual-level parameters were drawn from normal distributions around the population means (see `scripts/20_prepare_simulated_data.R` for details). We then fitted the EZ-Diffusion 3par, Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk), and full DDM to these data following the same `bmm` workflow used in the tutorials. We set two a-priori criteria for successful recovery: at the group level, the 95% credible interval for each parameter should contain its generating value (calibration); at the subject level, true and recovered values should correlate at $r > .70$, the conventional benchmark for treating a measure as a reliable individual-difference index. Of the two, the subject-level criterion is the practically more important one: absolute calibration can only be evaluated in simulations, whereas ordering individuals correctly is what applied uses of DDM parameters, as predictors, covariates, or outcomes, rely on.

## Group-Level Recovery

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-group
#| fig-cap: "Group-level parameter recovery. Points indicate posterior means for each estimation approach; error bars show 95% credible intervals. Dashed lines mark the true generating values. All three approaches recover drift; the Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) places bound below its generating value."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_group.pdf"))
```

All three estimation approaches recovered drift within their 95% credible intervals in both conditions (@fig-recovery-group). The EZ-Diffusion Model and the full DDM also recovered bound, and both placed ndt marginally below its generating value of 0.3 s (`r rec_ndt_ez` s and `r rec_ndt_ddm` s). The competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald recovered ndt but placed bound `r rec_crisk_bound_pct`% below its generating value of 1.5 (`r rec_crisk_bound`) and $\zeta_r$ slightly below 0.5 (`r rec_crisk_zr`). On the lexical decision data, by contrast, its bound agreed with the full DDM's (Part III), so the two results together say that the competing-risks bound is not guaranteed to match the full DDM's.

## Subject-Level Recovery

Beyond group-level means, we evaluated whether the models recover individual differences by correlating true participant-level parameters with their posterior estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-subject
#| fig-cap: "Subject-level parameter recovery. Each point represents one participant's recovered posterior mean plotted against its true generating value (x-axis); vertical bars show the 95% credible interval of the individual-level posterior. High correlations indicate that the estimation approaches preserve the rank ordering of individual differences. Columns show drift (easy and hard conditions), bound, and ndt; rows show the three estimation approaches."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_subject.pdf"))
```

Subject-level correlations between true and recovered parameters were high across all estimation approaches (@fig-recovery-subject), ranging from $r$ = `r recovery_r_min` to `r recovery_r_max` (median $r$ = `r recovery_r_median`). These strong correlations indicate that the hierarchical structure in `bmm` preserves individual differences while borrowing strength across participants, an essential property for studies that use DDM parameters as individual difference measures. The results are consistent with published recovery studies and confirm that all three `bmm` estimation approaches produce reliable estimates at both the group and individual level under controlled conditions.


## Subject-Level Recovery With a Biased Starting Point

The recovery study of Part I adds a second dataset, with two stimulus types and a starting point of 0.60 or 0.40 by bias condition, fitted with the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, the three-parameter model, and the full DDM. @fig-bias-recovery-subject shows the subject-level scatter plots; the correlations are reported in Part I.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-recovery-subject
#| fig-cap: "Subject-level recovery with a biased starting point. Each point is one participant's recovered posterior mean against its generating value; vertical bars show the 95% credible interval. Columns show drift (stimulus A and B), bound, ndt, and the relative starting point (bias conditions A and B); rows show the four-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, the three-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model, and the full DDM."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
if (bias_ok) {
  knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "22_bias_recovery_subject.pdf"))
} else {
  ggplot() + annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0, label = "Figure pending: scripts/22_bias_recovery.R has not been run yet.") + theme_void()
}
```
